overview: Pergamon, above modern Bergama in western Turkey, became the Attalid dynasty’s capital and a celebrated center of learning and art. Its hillside buildings joined royal ambition with impressive engineering. This card follows the late kingdom and its transition into the Roman world.

periods.title: An established Attalid kingdom
periods.summary: The map opens late in Attalos I’s reign; Eumenes II succeeded him in 197 BCE.

periods.title: Expansion and royal building
periods.summary: The settlement of Apameia enlarged Attalid territory; Eumenes II and his successors supported cities and cultural institutions.

periods.title: A contested bequest
periods.summary: Attalos III left his kingdom to Rome, but Aristonikos challenged the transfer.

periods.title: Early Roman transition
periods.summary: The former kingdom became part of Roman Asia; Pergamon retained an important civic and cultural life.

items.text: The imported outline shows a restricted area of western Anatolia between 200 and 100 BCE. It does not show the Attalids’ full expanded territory. Its final decades also fall after the dynasty’s bequest to Rome: a changing regional history is hidden behind one map label.

Pergamon’s ruling family emerged from the struggles after Alexander the Great. Philetairos gained substantial independence in 281 BCE. Attalos I later took the royal title after defeating Galatian opponents. The kingdom was already generations old when this map record begins.

The settlement at Apameia in 188 BCE rewarded Rome’s Attalid ally with extensive former Seleucid lands. Holding them required further wars and cooperation with local communities. The new kingdom included Greek cities and diverse inland Anatolian populations.

The capital climbed a steep hill. Builders used terraces for sanctuaries, colonnades and public buildings, while the theatre fitted the slope. Looking impressive here required serious work with the landscape: a royal building project could also be a stair-climbing project.

Courtyards shaped domestic space. Monika Trümper’s survey counted 18 courtyard houses and 21 houses with columned courtyards at Pergamon, including palaces; most originated in the Hellenistic centuries. These different-sized homes give a much broader picture of residents’ surroundings than the royal monuments alone.

A bathroom in every house? The same survey identified no securely Hellenistic bathroom in those 39 dwellings. Some large houses gained elaborate bathing rooms much later, from the late first century BCE. Ancient washing could use portable basins; absence of a dedicated room does not mean absence of washing.

Everyday clay objects depended on nearby craftspeople. Research covering Hellenistic and Roman Pergamon finds that regional workshops supplied most pottery. Archaeologists compare clay under magnification and use chemical analysis to separate local products from imports. A broken pot can preserve a surprisingly useful workshop address.

Water reached the hill through ambitious pipelines. The Madradağ system, dated around 180 to 160 BCE, ran approximately 42 kilometers. Engineer Günther Garbrecht estimated that it required about 200,000 individual pipe sections. Supplying a city also meant supplying potters with clay, fuel and an enormous production job.

Pipe fragments still raise questions. A 2022 field report describes pieces with different clay fabrics, shapes and stamps near an aqueduct. Some marks resemble those of other known pipelines. Researchers are testing how the pieces belong together, rather like solving a plumbing puzzle with most of the instructions missing.

A large cistern near the palaces measured roughly 4.55 meters across and 6.20 meters deep. One engineering study interprets it as a water reserve for fighting fires. In that reconstruction, people passed water along human chains: an emergency service powered by neighbors and buckets.

Eumenes II’s gymnasium spread over three terraces, with running tracks and an open exercise court. A public fountain stood by its western entrance. Streets of the expanding city led toward it, making exercise and civic gathering a central part of Pergamon’s urban plan.

The royal treasury supported the gymnasium’s oil fund. After the dynasty ended, responsibility passed to the gymnasium’s official. Physical training required a budget as well as enthusiasm; this institution was a meeting point between royal finance and civic life.

At Metropolis, another city in the kingdom, inscriptions record an annual royal allocation of 500 drachmas for lessons for freeborn young people, alongside a separate oil fund. Education had its own line in the budget, though this was not schooling available equally to everyone.

The library displayed a large marble Athena modeled on the famous gold-and-ivory goddess in Athens. The Pergamene version, from the second century BCE, linked books and scholarship with a deity of arts and knowledge. Royal learning was also public image-making: the kings wanted their city compared with Athens.

People seeking healing could visit the sanctuary of Asklepios outside the city. A sleeping or incubation area developed in the third century BCE; worshippers hoped for the god’s help through dreams. Early in the second century, colonnades enclosed the sanctuary and a sacred road connected it with Pergamon.

The Great Altar, dated approximately 180 to 160 BCE, carried a dramatic carved battle between gods and giants. Another frieze told the story of Telephos, the city’s mythical founder. The monument joined religious offerings, spectacular storytelling and a royal claim to an impressive ancestry.

Palace mosaic-makers used tiny cut stones, colored stones and glass instead of relying only on pebbles. Fine picture panels could be made in a workshop and inserted into a floor afterward. One royal mosaic includes a vividly colored parakeet: luxury decoration at your feet.

A real Greek signature survives in the Hephaistion mosaic from Palace V: ΗΦΑΙΣΤΙΩΝ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ, meaning “Hephaistion made [it].” These are modern printed letters transcribing the Hellenistic mosaic inscription. They preserve a craftsperson’s name, not just a king’s.

The signature is itself a visual joke. Its letters appear on a little piece of parchment represented in stone, held down at the corners, with one corner curling upward and casting a shadow. The floor pretends to have a loose note on it. Please do not tidy away the artwork!

Attalos II also paid for a great market building in Athens during his reign, 159 to 138 BCE. It had two storeys, each with 21 shops behind a colonnade. Such gifts let a king’s reputation travel abroad while providing real places to trade, walk and meet.

ending.text: Attalos III’s bequest in 133 BCE did not create a peaceful instant handover. Aristonikos rebelled before Roman provincial rule was established after 129 BCE. Pergamon itself was not destroyed in that transition and retained civic privileges under Rome. The kingdom ended, but the city and its cultural life continued beyond the map’s 100 BCE endpoint.
